visual.caption: Every long-term source is either owners' money or borrowed money.

slides.narration: Every long term source is either owners' money or borrowed money. Owners' funds include equity shares, preference shares and retained earnings. Borrowed funds include debentures and long term loans. Bonus, rights, employee options, sweat equity and placements are simply ways of issuing shares.

slides.heading: Equity shares: features

rows: Holders own the company and elect its directors
Paid last, from what is left
Depends on profit and the board
Repaid only on winding up (or a buy-back)
Gains most in good years, loses most in bad

visual.alt: Table of five features of equity shares with their meanings

slides.narration: Equity shareholders are the real owners. They vote and elect directors. They are paid last, so their claim is residual. Their dividend rises and falls with profit. Their capital stays with the company until it is wound up. They bear the highest risk, and can enjoy the highest reward.

slides.heading: Equity: for and against
columns:
**For the company**

No fixed burden; permanent; assets stay free; a strong base for borrowing.

**Against**

Dilutes control; expensive; costly to issue; risk of raising too much.

rows: Costlier: investors expect more; no tax shield
High floatation cost and long formalities

visual.alt: Table of four advantages and four disadvantages of equity shares to the issuing company

slides.narration: For the company, equity is comfortable: no fixed dividend, no repayment and no charge on assets. But it has costs. New shareholders share control. Investors expect a high return, and dividends save no tax. A public issue is costly and slow.

slides.heading: Quick check: equity and borrowing
slides.body_md: True or false: a large equity base makes it easier for a company to borrow.
slides.narration: Think about how lenders feel when owners have a lot at stake.

slides.heading: Preference shares and their types
slides.body_md: Preference shares get a **fixed dividend** and **return of capital before** equity; their **vote is restricted**.

rows: Shares surplus profit / fixed dividend only
Repaid after a period; Indian companies may issue only redeemable preference shares

visual.alt: Table of the types of preference shares in pairs with the difference between each pair; Indian companies may now issue only redeemable preference shares

slides.narration: Preference shareholders come first for a fixed dividend and for repayment of capital. In return, they vote only on matters affecting them, unless their dividend has been unpaid for two years or more. Their types come in pairs: cumulative or not, participating or not, convertible or not. Indian companies may now issue only redeemable ones.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: cumulative arrears
slides.body_md: An imagined battery maker missed its preference dividend for two years.
bullets: Step 1: annual dividend = number × face value × rate.
Step 2: add each unpaid year to **arrears**.
Step 3: in the paying year, clear arrears **plus** the current year before any equity dividend.

visual.alt: Worked table for imagined cumulative preference shares: eighty thousand rupees due each year; nothing paid in years one and two, so arrears build to one lakh sixty thousand; in year three two lakh forty thousand must be paid before any equity dividend
visual.caption: Imagined: Bhadra Batteries Ltd, 10,000 cumulative 8 per cent preference shares of ₹100.

slides.narration: Ten thousand shares of one hundred rupees at eight per cent need eighty thousand rupees a year. Nothing was paid in years one and two, so arrears build up. In year three the company must pay all three years, two lakh forty thousand rupees, before equity holders get a single rupee.

slides.heading: Quick check: shares that change
slides.body_md: Preference shares that become equity shares after five years are…
slides.narration: What does the share turn into, and what is that called?

slides.heading: Equity versus preference

visual.alt: Table distinguishing equity and preference shares on dividend, priority, voting, risk, repayment and arrears

slides.narration: Compare the two on six bases. Equity dividend varies; preference dividend is fixed. Preference comes first; equity comes last. Equity votes fully; preference votes only in limited cases. Equity is riskier. Preference shares are redeemable, and cumulative ones can build arrears.

slides.heading: Five special ways of issuing shares

rows: Existing shareholders, in proportion, usually below market price; can be renounced
Employees, as an option at a pre-set price after a vesting period
Directors or employees, for know-how or intellectual property
Qualified institutional buyers, by a listed company

visual.alt: Table of five methods of issuing shares, who receives the shares and whether fresh funds come in

slides.narration: Bonus shares are free shares made out of reserves. A rights issue offers new shares to existing holders, usually below market price, and the right can be sold. An employee stock option lets staff buy later at a set price. Sweat equity rewards know how. A qualified institutional placement lets a listed company raise money quickly from big institutions.

visual.caption: A bonus issue moves reserves; a rights issue brings in money.

slides.narration: Here is the key difference. In a bonus issue, money already held as reserves is relabelled as share capital, so no cash comes in. In a rights issue, shareholders pay cash, so the company receives fresh funds. Rights can be renounced; bonus shares cannot.

bullets: Step 2: for rights, multiply by the **issue price**.

rows: Asha: 500 shares of Pushkar Prints Ltd
Farhan: 400 shares of Indravati Infra Ltd

visual.alt: Worked table: a holder of five hundred shares receives two hundred free bonus shares in the ratio two to five; a holder of four hundred shares in a one-for-four rights issue at sixty rupees gets one hundred shares and pays six thousand rupees
visual.caption: Bonus: free, no cash to the company. Rights: paid, fresh cash to the company.

slides.narration: Asha holds five hundred shares and gets bonus shares at two for every five, so she receives two hundred free shares. Farhan holds four hundred shares and is offered one for every four at sixty rupees. He gets one hundred shares and pays six thousand rupees.

slides.heading: Quick check: rewarding know-how
slides.body_md: Shares given without cash to a director who developed a patented process are…
slides.narration: The reward is for effort and know-how, not money.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Owners; votes; residual claim; permanent; no fixed burden
Fixed dividend and capital first; restricted vote; redeemable
Bonus (free), rights (paid), ESOP, sweat equity, QIP

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: equity shares, preference shares, their types and the special methods of issuing shares

slides.narration: To sum up. Equity shareholders own the company, vote and take the residual profit. Preference shareholders get a fixed dividend and capital first, with a restricted vote. Preference shares may be cumulative, participating, convertible and redeemable. Bonus, rights, ESOP, sweat equity and QIP are five special ways of issuing shares.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: In case questions, look for **free** (bonus), **existing holders, paid** (rights), **employees, option** (ESOP), **know-how** (sweat equity), **institutions, listed** (QIP).
For distinctions, write **basis by basis**, not two separate paragraphs.
Show working for **ratios** step by step.

visual.alt: Three steps for case questions: spot the clue, name the source or type, and explain why

slides.narration: Some tips. Learn the clue words that reveal each type of issue. When asked to distinguish, set your answer out basis by basis, so the examiner sees each contrast. And show the working for every ratio question.

decks.title: Long-term Sources — Part 2: Retained Earnings, Debentures and Term Loans
goals: Evaluate retained earnings as a source of finance
Describe kinds of debentures and distinguish shares from debentures
State the advantages and disadvantages of loans from banks and financial institutions

slides.heading: Retained Earnings, Debentures and Loans
slides.body_md: Part 2: **ploughing back** profit, borrowing through **debentures**, and **term loans** from banks and institutions.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: retained earnings, debentures, and loans from banks and financial institutions
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In part two we look at money the company keeps from its own profits, and at money it borrows: debentures sold to investors, and loans from banks and financial institutions.

slides.heading: Retained earnings
slides.body_md: **Retained earnings** (ploughing back) is the part of profit kept in the business instead of being paid as dividend.

visual.alt: Table of four merits and four demerits of retained earnings

slides.narration: Retained earnings are an internal source of owners' funds. They are permanent, cost nothing to raise and bring in no new owners. They also build credit and a cushion for bad years. But shareholders may resent low dividends, the amount depends on profit, and managers may treat the money as free.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how much is ploughed back?
slides.body_md: An imagined hosiery company decides its dividend.
bullets: Step 1: find the **dividend** = payout ratio × profit after tax.

visual.alt: Worked table: an imagined company with profit after tax of fifty lakh rupees pays forty per cent as dividend, twenty lakh rupees, and ploughs back thirty lakh rupees
visual.caption: Retained = profit after tax − dividend.

slides.narration: The company earns fifty lakh rupees after tax and pays forty per cent as dividend, which is twenty lakh rupees. The remaining thirty lakh rupees are ploughed back to buy knitting machines.

slides.heading: Quick check: ploughing back
slides.body_md: Retained earnings as a source of finance means…
slides.narration: Where does the money come from?

slides.heading: Debentures and their kinds
slides.body_md: A **debenture** is an acknowledgement of **debt** with a **fixed rate of interest**; its holder is a **creditor**.

visual.alt: Table of kinds of debentures by security, repayment, conversion and registration

slides.narration: A debenture is a loan to the company, split into small units sold to investors. Debentures are classified by security, repayment, conversion and registration. They may be secured or not, redeemable or not, convertible in full, in part or not at all, and registered or payable to bearer.

slides.heading: Debentures: for and against
columns:
**For the company**

No dilution of control; interest saves tax; fixed cost allows trading on equity; redeemable when not needed.

**Against**

Fixed interest even in bad years; charge on assets limits further borrowing; repayment burden.

visual.alt: Table of three advantages and three disadvantages of debentures to the company

slides.narration: Debentures keep control with the owners, and interest saves tax. When the business earns more than the interest rate, they raise returns to shareholders. But interest must be paid even in a loss year, pledged assets cannot back other loans, and the money must be repaid.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: after-tax cost of debentures
slides.body_md: An imagined wire company issues 9 per cent debentures; tax is 25 per cent.
bullets: Step 2: tax saved = interest × tax rate.
Step 3: after-tax cost = net interest ÷ amount × 100.

visual.alt: Worked table: twenty lakh rupees of nine per cent debentures cost one lakh eighty thousand rupees of interest; with tax at twenty-five per cent the net cost is one lakh thirty-five thousand rupees, an after-tax cost of six point seven five per cent
visual.caption: The tax saving on interest is why debt is cheaper than preference or equity capital.

slides.narration: Twenty lakh rupees at nine per cent means one lakh eighty thousand rupees of interest. Because interest is deducted before tax, a quarter of it comes back as tax saved. The net cost is one lakh thirty five thousand rupees, or six point seven five per cent.

slides.heading: Quick check: do lenders vote?
slides.body_md: True or false: debenture holders vote at general meetings.
slides.narration: Are debenture holders owners or creditors?

slides.heading: Shares versus debentures

visual.alt: Table distinguishing shares and debentures on status, return, loss-year payment, tax, voting, security and priority on winding up

slides.narration: Shareholders are owners; debenture holders are creditors. Shareholders get dividends, which may vary; debenture holders get fixed interest, even in a loss year. Interest saves tax, dividends do not. Shareholders vote; debenture holders do not. Debentures are usually secured and are repaid first on winding up.

slides.heading: Loans from banks and financial institutions
slides.body_md: **Term loans** run for more than a year, are repaid in **instalments** and are usually **secured**. Financial institutions also offer **advice**.

rows: Fixed interest and instalments even in bad years
Institutions add technical advice; available in depressed markets

visual.alt: Table of advantages and disadvantages of term loans from commercial banks and financial institutions

slides.narration: Banks and specialised financial institutions give term loans for projects. Loans are private, so plans stay confidential, and they bring no new owners. Institutions often add technical advice and lend even when share markets are weak. But they want security, careful appraisal and sometimes a director on the board.

slides.heading: Quick check: keeping plans private
slides.body_md: A company wants long-term funds without publishing a prospectus. Why does a term loan suit it?
slides.narration: Who learns about the company's plans in a loan?

slides.heading: Choosing a long-term source

nodes.label: Steady cash flow and assets to pledge?
Equity, or retained earnings if available

visual.alt: Decision flow: a company needing long-term funds asks whether it must keep control; if yes, and it has steady cash flow and assets to pledge, debentures or a term loan suit it; otherwise equity, or retained earnings if available
visual.caption: A simple way to reason about the choice; real decisions weigh several factors together.

slides.narration: Here is one way to reason. If owners must keep control, and the company has steady cash flow and assets to pledge, debentures or a term loan suit it. If not, equity is safer, and retained earnings are best of all when profits allow. Real decisions weigh cost, risk and control together.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Ploughed-back profit; cheap and permanent, but uncertain
Debt; fixed interest; secured, convertible, redeemable, registered kinds
Owner vs creditor; dividend vs interest

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: retained earnings, debentures, shares versus debentures and term loans

slides.narration: To sum up. Retained earnings are cheap and permanent but uncertain. Debentures are debt with fixed interest, in several kinds. Shareholders own; debenture holders lend. Term loans are private and long term, but need security and come with conditions.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Say **owner** or **creditor** in every shares-versus-debentures answer.
Name debenture kinds **by basis**: security, repayment, conversion, registration.
For loans, mention **security** and **restrictive conditions** as drawbacks.
In numericals, remember that interest saves **tax**; dividends do not.

visual.alt: Three steps for case questions: spot the clue, name the source or type, and explain why

slides.narration: Final tips. Always state who is an owner and who is a creditor. Classify debentures basis by basis. Remember security and conditions as the price of a loan. And in any cost calculation, let interest, but not dividends, reduce tax.

sections.heading: 1. Equity shares
sections.body_md:
**Equity shares** represent ownership of a company. **Features:** ownership and voting rights; residual claim on income and assets; dividend not fixed; permanent capital (repaid only on winding up, apart from a buy-back); limited liability; highest risk.

**Advantages to the company:** no fixed burden of dividend; permanent capital; no charge on assets; a strong equity base improves creditworthiness; suits investors willing to take risk.

**Disadvantages:** dilution of control; costlier than debt (higher expected return, dividend not tax-deductible); high floatation cost and formalities; risk of over-capitalisation; may encourage speculation in the shares.

key_terms.definition_md: A share giving ownership, votes and a residual claim.
The right to what remains after all prior claims are met.
Cost of issuing securities: fees, printing, advertising, underwriting.

sections.heading: 2. Preference shares
sections.body_md:
**Preference shares** carry a preferential right to a **fixed dividend** and to **return of capital** on winding up, before equity. Their **voting rights are restricted** to matters directly affecting them, but extend to all resolutions if their dividend is unpaid for two years or more (Companies Act, 2013).

**Types:** cumulative / non-cumulative; participating / non-participating; convertible / non-convertible; redeemable. Under the Companies Act, 2013 a company may **not** issue irredeemable preference shares; they must be redeemed, normally within twenty years.

**Advantages to the company:** no dilution of control; fixed dividend allows trading on equity; no charge on assets; attracts cautious investors.
**Disadvantages:** dividend is not tax-deductible, so costlier than debt; arrears burden on cumulative shares; fixed dividend reduces what is left for equity.

**Equity versus preference:** dividend (variable / fixed); priority (last / first); voting (full / restricted); risk (high / lower); redemption (no / yes); arrears (none / possible).

key_terms.definition_md: Shares surplus profit beyond its fixed dividend.
Can be converted into equity after a stated period.

sections.heading: 3. Bonus shares, rights issue, ESOP, sweat equity and QIP
sections.body_md:
- **Bonus shares:** free shares to existing shareholders by **capitalising reserves** (free reserves or securities premium). No fresh funds.
- **Rights issue:** new shares offered to **existing shareholders in proportion** to their holdings, usually below market price; the right can be **renounced**.
- **ESOP (employee stock option plan):** an option to employees to buy shares at a **pre-determined price** after a vesting period.
- **Sweat equity shares:** shares issued to directors or employees at a discount or **for non-cash consideration** such as know-how, intellectual property or value addition.
- **QIP (qualified institutional placement):** a **listed** company issues shares or convertible securities to **qualified institutional buyers** (mutual funds, banks, insurers and similar), quickly and without a full public issue.

**Bonus versus rights:** funds (none / fresh cash); payment (free / paid); renunciation (not possible / possible); source (reserves / shareholders' cash).

sections.heading: 4. Retained earnings
sections.body_md:
**Retained earnings** (ploughing back of profits) are the part of net profit kept in the business. It is an **internal** source of owners' funds.

**Merits:** permanent; no floatation cost; no dilution of control; improves credit standing; provides a cushion that helps keep dividends steady.
**Demerits:** low dividends may cause dissatisfaction; uncertain, because it depends on profit; opportunity cost may be ignored, leading to careless use; possible misuse by management.

sections.heading: 5. Debentures
sections.body_md:
A **debenture** is a written acknowledgement of **debt** by a company, carrying a **fixed rate of interest**. Holders are **creditors** with no vote.

**Kinds:** secured / unsecured; redeemable / irredeemable; fully convertible / partly convertible / non-convertible; registered / bearer.

**Advantages to the company:** no dilution of control; interest is tax-deductible, so cheaper; fixed cost permits trading on equity; can be redeemed when funds are no longer needed; suits cautious investors.
**Disadvantages:** fixed interest burden even in a loss year; charge on assets reduces further borrowing capacity; redemption must be provided for; risky when earnings are unstable.

**Shares versus debentures:** status (owner / creditor); return (dividend / interest); loss-year payment (no / yes); tax (not deductible / deductible); voting (yes / no); security (none / usually secured); priority on winding up (after creditors / before shareholders).

sections.heading: 6. Loans from commercial banks and financial institutions
sections.body_md:
**Term loans** from commercial banks are given for more than a year, usually against security, and repaid in instalments. **Financial institutions** (development banks and state-level corporations) provide medium- and long-term project finance, often with technical and managerial advice.

**Advantages:** long-term funds without a public issue; confidentiality; no dilution of control; flexible repayment in instalments; advice from institutions; available when markets are depressed.
**Disadvantages:** security required; lengthy appraisal and documentation; restrictive conditions such as a nominee director or limits on dividends and further borrowing; fixed repayment burden.

**Reason (R):** Retained earnings are an external source of finance.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The assertion is true: heavy retention means lower dividends. The reason is false: retained earnings are an internal source.

questions.stem_md: Hooghly Hosiery Ltd (imagined) earns a profit after tax of ₹50,00,000 and pays 40 per cent of it as dividend. How much does it plough back into the business (in ₹)?
Hooghly Hosiery Ltd (imagined) ploughed back ₹30 lakh of profit to buy knitting machines. State two merits of this source for the company.
questions.solution_md: Two merits (permanent, no cost of raising, no dilution, credit standing, cushion for bad years) linked to the case.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Permanent and cheap:** the ₹30 lakh needs **no repayment** and involves **no floatation cost**.
2. **No loss of control:** no new shares are issued, so **ownership stays the same**.

questions.stem_md: For three years Krishna Kitchenware Ltd (imagined) has kept almost all its profit and paid a tiny dividend; this year its profit fell sharply. Explain three demerits of relying on retained earnings that this case shows.
questions.solution_md: Three demerits (dissatisfaction, uncertainty, opportunity cost, possible misuse) linked to the case.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Shareholder dissatisfaction:** a **tiny dividend** for three years may anger shareholders and depress the share price.
2. **Uncertain source:** when **profit fell sharply**, little could be retained, so funds dried up.
3. **Opportunity cost ignored:** managers may treat retained funds as **free** and use them carelessly.

questions.stem_md: A debenture is

options.text_md: a certificate of part-ownership of a company
an acknowledgement of debt by a company, carrying a fixed rate of interest
a free share given out of reserves
a short-term advance from a customer

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** an acknowledgement of debt by a company, carrying a fixed rate of interest. A debenture holder is a creditor of the company and receives a fixed interest, not a dividend.

questions.stem_md: Periyar Polymers Ltd (imagined) issues debentures backed by a charge on its factory, so holders can sell the factory to recover their money if it defaults. These debentures are
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** secured debentures. Debentures backed by a charge on specific assets are secured.

questions.stem_md: Rann Renewables Ltd (imagined) issues debentures of which ₹600 of each ₹1,000 will be turned into equity shares after three years and ₹400 will be repaid in cash. These are
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** partly convertible debentures. Only part of each debenture converts into equity; the rest is redeemed in cash: partly convertible.

questions.stem_md: How do registered debentures differ from bearer debentures?

options.text_md: Holders' names are recorded by the company and transfer needs a transfer deed; bearer debentures pass by mere delivery

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Holders' names are recorded by the company and transfer needs a transfer deed; bearer debentures pass by mere delivery. Registered debentures are recorded in the company's register and transferred formally; bearer debentures are transferable by delivery.

questions.stem_md: Satpura Ceramics Ltd (imagined) earns 16 per cent on its capital and has steady sales. Which reason **best** explains why it may prefer 9 per cent debentures to new equity?

options.text_md: Debentures give holders a vote, which shareholders like
Debentures never have to be repaid
Fixed-cost debt lets it trade on equity, and interest is tax-deductible
Debenture interest is paid only in profitable years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Fixed-cost debt lets it trade on equity, and interest is tax-deductible. With a 16 per cent return against 9 per cent interest and steady sales, debt raises earnings per share, and interest saves tax.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Debentures can be a heavy burden on a company in a bad year.

**Reason (R):** Interest on debentures must be paid whether or not the company earns a profit.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and the fixed, compulsory interest is exactly why debentures weigh heavily when profits fall.

questions.stem_md: Debenture holders have the right to vote at the general meetings of the company.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Debenture holders are creditors, not owners, and have no voting rights.

questions.stem_md: Wardha Wires Ltd (imagined) issues ₹20,00,000 of 9 per cent debentures. Its tax rate is 25 per cent. Calculate the after-tax cost of these debentures as a percentage of the amount raised (ignore issue expenses).
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Interest = 20,00,000 × 0.09 = ₹1,80,000.
Step 2: Tax saved = 25 per cent, so net cost = 1,80,000 × 0.75 = ₹1,35,000.
Step 3: After-tax cost = 1,35,000 ÷ 20,00,000 × 100 = 6.75 per cent.

questions.stem_md: Match each kind of debenture with its description.

match_right.text_md: Backed by a charge on assets
Repaid in cash; never become equity

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Secured: charge on assets; unsecured: no charge; non-convertible: cash repayment only; bearer: pass by delivery.

questions.stem_md: Asha holds equity shares and Farhan holds debentures of Mahi Motorcycles Ltd (imagined). Distinguish their positions on status and return.
questions.solution_md: Status and return distinguished for the two holders.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Status:** Asha is an **owner** of the company; Farhan is a **creditor** who has lent it money.
2. **Return:** Asha gets a **dividend** that varies with profit; Farhan gets **fixed interest** even in a loss year.

questions.stem_md: Indravati Infra Ltd (imagined) offers investors three choices: debentures secured on its toll road, debentures that turn into shares after four years, and debentures repayable in year seven. Name and explain each kind.
questions.solution_md: Secured, convertible and redeemable debentures named and explained from the case.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Secured debentures:** backed by a **charge on the toll road**, which holders can sell if the company defaults.
2. **Convertible debentures:** they **turn into equity shares** after four years.
3. **Redeemable debentures:** the company **repays them** on a fixed date, in year seven.

questions.stem_md:
Satpura Ceramics Ltd (imagined) has steady sales, earns well above the interest rate and owns a large, unpledged factory. It is choosing between equity and secured debentures for ₹25 crore.
(a) Distinguish between shares and debentures on three bases. [3]
(b) Explain two reasons why debentures could suit Satpura Ceramics. [2]
questions.solution_md: Three bases; two reasons linked to the case.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Status:** a shareholder is an **owner**; a debenture holder is a **creditor**.
**Return:** shareholders receive a **dividend** out of profit, which may vary; debenture holders receive **fixed interest**, payable even in a loss year.
**Security and priority:** debentures are usually **secured** on assets and repaid **before** shareholders on winding up; shares carry no security.

(b) **Trading on equity and tax:** since it **earns well above the interest rate**, debt raises earnings per share, and interest is **tax-deductible**. **Security available:** its large **unpledged factory** can back secured debentures, so investors will accept a lower rate, and its steady sales make the fixed interest safe to pay.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Two reasons linked to the case

questions.stem_md: Specialised financial institutions (such as development banks and state financial corporations) differ from ordinary lenders mainly because they

options.text_md: provide long-term finance for projects and often give technical and managerial advice too
lend only for less than a week
buy and sell shares on behalf of the public

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** provide long-term finance for projects and often give technical and managerial advice too. Financial institutions were set up to provide medium- and long-term project finance, often with advice, where ordinary sources fall short.

questions.stem_md: Sutlej Seeds Ltd (imagined) needs ₹8 crore for a cold store but does not want to publish a prospectus or disclose its plans to rivals. A term loan from a bank suits it mainly because a loan

options.text_md: is raised privately, without public disclosure

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** is raised privately, without public disclosure. A loan is a private arrangement between borrower and lender, so the company's plans stay confidential.

questions.stem_md: A financial institution lends ₹50 crore to Indravati Infra Ltd (imagined) on condition that it appoints a nominee director to the board and pays no dividend above 10 per cent until the loan is repaid. These conditions show a **disadvantage** of institutional loans:

options.text_md: restrictive terms that limit management's freedom

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** restrictive terms that limit management's freedom. Institutions often impose covenants such as nominee directors and dividend limits, which restrict the company's freedom.

questions.stem_md: When the share market is depressed and a public issue would fail, Pushkar Prints Ltd (imagined) can still raise long-term funds through a term loan from a financial institution.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Loans do not depend on investors' mood in the share market, so they remain available when public issues are difficult.

questions.stem_md: A bank loan for a period of more than a year, repaid in instalments and usually secured on the asset bought, is called a ___ loan.
questions.solution_md: It is a term loan: a loan for a fixed period, repaid in instalments.

questions.stem_md: Krishna Kitchenware Ltd (imagined) is choosing a seven-year term loan from a financial institution for its new plant. Explain two advantages of this source for the company.
questions.solution_md: Two advantages (long-term funds, advice, confidentiality, no dilution, flexible repayment, availability in depressed markets) applied.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Advice and support:** the institution often gives **technical and managerial guidance** on the new plant.
2. **No dilution:** a loan brings **no new shareholders**, so control stays with existing owners; repayment can be **spread over seven years**.

questions.stem_md: Before lending ₹12 crore to Bhadra Batteries Ltd (imagined), a bank asks for a mortgage on its plant, detailed project reports and a ban on further borrowing. Explain three disadvantages of bank and institutional loans shown here.
questions.solution_md: Three disadvantages (security, procedure, restrictive covenants, fixed repayment burden) linked to the case.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Security required:** the bank wants a **mortgage on the plant**, so these assets cannot be offered to back any other loan later.
2. **Lengthy procedure:** preparing **detailed project reports** for appraisal takes weeks and adds cost.
3. **Restrictive conditions:** the **ban on further borrowing** limits management's freedom to raise funds when a new need arises.

questions.stem_md:
Satpura Ceramics Ltd (imagined) is listed and has large free reserves. Its board is considering a bonus issue, a rights issue and a QIP, and wants to reward a director who developed a new glaze.
(a) Distinguish between a bonus issue and a rights issue on two bases. [2]
(b) Explain the meaning of sweat equity and QIP, and say which purpose each serves for this company. [3]
questions.solution_md: Two bases; sweat equity and QIP explained and matched to purposes.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Fresh funds:** a bonus issue brings in **no new money**, as reserves are capitalised; a rights issue **raises cash** from existing shareholders.
**Renunciation:** bonus shares are free and **cannot be renounced**; rights can be **renounced** in favour of others.

(b) **Sweat equity** means shares issued to directors or employees at a discount or **for non-cash consideration** such as know-how or intellectual property. It suits **rewarding the director** for the new glaze without paying cash.
**QIP** means a **listed** company placing shares or convertible securities with **qualified institutional buyers** such as mutual funds and insurers, without a full public issue. It suits Satpura if it needs a **large sum quickly**, for example to build a new kiln line.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Sweat equity and QIP explained, each with its purpose

questions.stem_md:
Hooghly Hosiery Ltd (imagined) can fund a ₹6 crore dyeing unit either from retained profit or with a term loan from a bank.
(a) Explain two merits and one demerit of using retained earnings. [3]
(b) Explain two disadvantages of the term loan for the company. [2]
questions.solution_md: Two merits and one demerit of retained earnings; two disadvantages of a term loan.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Merits:** retained profit involves **no floatation cost**, since there is no prospectus or underwriting, and it brings **no new shareholders**, so control is not diluted. **Demerit:** using ₹6 crore of profit for the unit means **lower dividends**, which may make shareholders unhappy and weaken the share price.

(b) **Fixed repayment burden:** the bank must be paid **interest and instalments** on schedule, even if hosiery sales fall in a bad year. **Security and conditions:** the bank will want a **mortgage** on the dyeing unit and may impose **restrictive conditions**, such as limits on further borrowing or on dividends, which reduce management's freedom.
